comment: Validation oracles: the published specifications whose own examples are the Prism's test content. tools/oracle/gen.py fetches each source at its pinned SHA-256, takes its examples out mechanically (an example is kept only if every address in it is at a domain reserved for documentation, RFC 2606 and RFC 6761, so no real person's address enters the repository), and reads each one with a reference reader written to the source's own grammar. test/oracle/read.test.mjs then holds the Prism's reading (site/card.mjs readItem) to that reading, field by field: a message's title, sender, time and plain words; an event's title, place and start; a card's name; a header's encoded words as the specification says they display; a base64 test vector as it decodes; a CSV example as RFC 4180 reads it; a one-time code message as the WICG report says. gaps: kinds of content the Prism reads that no published specification gives examples of, each with why; no test content is written for them. Nothing here is invented: a new kind of content is added by naming the specification it follows.

sources.title: RFC 5322 Internet Message Format, Appendix A
RFC 2047 MIME Part Three: Message Header Extensions for Non-ASCII Text, Section 8 Examples
RFC 4648 The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings, Section 10 Test Vectors
RFC 4180 Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files, Section 2
WICG Origin-bound one-time codes delivered via SMS, Authoring examples

gaps.why: No published specification gives example card numbers: ISO/IEC 7812-1, which defines the issuer prefix and the Luhn check digit, is not freely published, and the networks' test numbers are on their own changing pages. The card detector (site/google/ingest.mjs) has no oracle test until one is pinned.
WhatsApp publishes no definition of its Export chat text format, only help pages on how to export. site/source/exports.mjs reads it, untested by any oracle.

Discord's help pages name the files of a data package (messages/index.json, messages/c<id>/messages.json or .csv) but publish no definition of their fields. Untested by any oracle; its CSV files follow RFC 4180, which is.
LinkedIn's help pages name messages.csv and Connections.csv but publish no definition of their columns. Untested by any oracle; the files follow RFC 4180, which is.
